Bull / bullish.long:
A bull expects prices to rise; "bullish" describes that view, or a market moving upward. The image is the animal thrusting up with its horns, the opposite motion to a bear's downward swipe.

The bull/bear pairing predates modern exchanges, tied to animal-baiting imagery from eighteenth-century London finance. It has survived because it compresses a directional stance into a single word.

The word carries no information about conviction, timeframe, or size. Someone bullish on a decade-long thesis and someone bullish on the next hour are using identical language for unrelated claims.

Where people get fooled: the label gets treated as analysis rather than a stance. A headline calling a market bullish states a direction, not a reason, and repetition can feel like accumulating evidence when none has actually accumulated.
Bull / bullish.usage: A trader might say they are 'bullish on gold into year-end' to describe a directional view, without specifying size, entry, or time horizon.

Bear / bearish.long:
A bear expects prices to fall; "bearish" describes that view, or a declining market. The image is a bear swiping downward, the mirror of the bull's upward horn.

Both terms have circulated in London finance since at least the early 1700s, well before any organised exchange discussed elsewhere in this glossary existed — among the oldest slang here by some margin.

Like bullish, the word says nothing about magnitude or timeframe. It is a stance, not a forecast with a defined size or a defined point at which it would be proven wrong.

Where people get fooled: persistent bearishness gets mistaken for caution or rigour. Staying bearish through a multi-year rally can look prudent right up until it is simply wrong, because the label never had to specify what would falsify it.
Bear / bearish.usage: Describing oneself as 'bearish' on a sector states a directional lean, not a risk-managed position with a defined size or exit.

Dip.long:
A dip is a short pullback within a larger uptrend: price falls, then, in the framing the word implies, resumes climbing. The term describes shape, and it does so after the fact.

Calling something a dip is a retrospective label. In real time, a falling price is simply a falling price; whether it becomes a dip or the start of a reversal is unknowable from inside the move itself.

The phrase is inseparable from "buy the dip", which turns a description into an instruction. That quiet conflation, between naming a shape and recommending an action, is where the term does most of its work.

Where people get fooled: a decline gets called a dip before the move has finished happening, borrowing confidence from every prior decline that recovered. The dips people remember are the ones that bounced, which makes the word feel safer than the actual base rate supports.
Dip.usage: Financial commentary often labels a decline a 'dip' well before the move has concluded, describing shape rather than predicting the outcome.

Bull trap.long:
A bull trap is a price move that breaks above resistance, draws in buyers expecting continuation, then reverses and falls, trapping those buyers in a losing long.

The mechanism is mechanical: a breakout attracts stop-loss orders and breakout buyers clustered above a level. Once that liquidity is taken, there may be no follow-through demand left to sustain the move further.

The term is applied after the fact, almost always to explain a loss. Very few traders describe a breakout as a bull trap while it is still working in their favour.

Where people get fooled: hindsight makes every failed breakout look obviously fake in retrospect, which invites overconfidence that the next one can be spotted in advance. At the time, most failed breakouts look identical to the ones that hold.
Bull trap.usage: A trader whose breakout purchase immediately reversed might describe the move afterwards as a bull trap.

Dead cat bounce.long:
A dead cat bounce is a brief price recovery within an ongoing downtrend, followed by the decline resuming. The name is old trading-floor gallows humour: even a dead cat bounces if it falls from high enough.

The phrase circulated widely in financial writing around the 1985 Singapore and Malaysian stock slump, though the underlying idea, a downtrend punctuated by short rallies, is far older than the label itself.

Like dip and bull trap, it is a shape-based label applied with hindsight. Nothing distinguishes a dead cat bounce from the start of a genuine recovery while the bounce is actually happening.

Where people get fooled: the term gets used to dismiss every rally within a downtrend as fake, which is its own bias running the opposite way. Some bounces are the actual bottom, and the label offers no way to tell which in advance.
Dead cat bounce.usage: A short rally during a prolonged decline is sometimes called a dead cat bounce, usually only after it has already failed.

Capitulation.long:
Capitulation is the point in a decline where remaining holders sell in bulk, typically near maximum fear, often marked by a sharp volume spike and an accelerating drop.

The mechanism combines forced and voluntary selling: margin calls, stop-losses, and plain panic converge in a short window, which can exhaust the pool of remaining sellers all at once.

It is another after-the-fact label. A low is called capitulation once it has held; almost no one calls it that with confidence while the selling is still under way.

Where people get fooled: people search for capitulation-shaped volume spikes to call a bottom in real time, but sharp volume spikes occur throughout downtrends, not only at the eventual low. Wanting an ending is not the same as identifying one.
Capitulation.usage: Commentators sometimes point to a volume spike during a crash and label it capitulation, typically once the low is already behind them.

Blow-off top.long:
A blow-off top describes a sharp, accelerating price rise late in an uptrend, often on heavy volume, followed by an equally sharp reversal, the mirror image of capitulation.

The pattern reflects late buying pressure arriving all at once, often from participants previously on the sidelines who are now chasing, which can exhaust fresh demand quickly once it is spent.

As with capitulation, the label is applied retrospectively. A steep rally only earns the term blow-off top once it has actually reversed, never confidently before that.

Where people get fooled: steep rallies that keep going get relabelled in hindsight as something else, a breakout or a re-rating, while the ones that reverse keep the blow-off top label. The pattern is only obvious once the outcome is known.
Blow-off top.usage: A parabolic move that reverses sharply is often described afterwards as a blow-off top.

Short squeeze.long:
A short squeeze is a rapid price rise driven by short-sellers being forced to buy back borrowed shares to close losing positions, which itself pushes the price higher still.

The mechanism is mechanical and well documented: rising prices increase losses on short positions, some shorts are forced out by margin calls or borrow recalls, and their buying adds further upward pressure, a feedback loop.

Short interest and days-to-cover figures give a measurable basis for the setup, unlike most slang here, which is why this term has genuine structural grounding rather than pure narrative.

Where people get fooled: high short interest is treated as a promise of a squeeze rather than a precondition for one. A squeeze also needs a trigger and buyers willing to hold through the volatility; short interest alone shows the fuel exists, not that anything ignites it.
Short squeeze.usage: Commentators cite elevated short interest and rising days-to-cover as squeeze conditions, without that data implying a squeeze is imminent.

Whale.long:
A whale is a market participant large enough that individual buying or selling moves price on its own, a term most common in crypto, where order books tend to be thinner.

Wallet-tracking tools make whale activity visible in crypto in a way it rarely is in equities, where large trades are more often broken up or routed through dark pools specifically to avoid detection.

The word is used loosely for any large holder, and separately, more speculatively, for one believed about to trade. That second use is speculation dressed up as observation.

Where people get fooled: a large wallet balance is treated as an imminent signal. Most whale balances sit unmoved for long stretches, and watching one while inferring intent from size alone is closer to narrative-building than to analysis.
Whale.usage: On-chain trackers flag large wallet movements as 'whale activity', describing size rather than confirming intent.

Pump and dump.long:
A pump and dump is a scheme where organisers inflate an asset's price through coordinated buying or hype, then sell into the demand they created, leaving later buyers holding the loss.

The mechanism predates crypto by a century in penny-stock form, and depends on information asymmetry: organisers know the exit is coming, buyers drawn in by the hype do not.

The term is now used both precisely, for coordinated schemes, and loosely, for any sharp rise and fall, which blurs a specific legal and structural claim into a vague insult.

Where people get fooled: by the time a move is obviously a pump, the dump is usually already close, because the visibility that makes it recognisable is the same hype that draws in the last round of buyers the organisers are selling to.
Pump and dump.usage: Regulators use 'pump and dump' as a specific term for coordinated manipulation schemes, distinct from its looser use for any sharp rise and fall.

Rug pull.long:
A rug pull is when a project's creators withdraw the funds or liquidity backing an asset and disappear, leaving holders with something worthless, most associated with crypto tokens and liquidity pools.

It is mechanically distinct from a pump and dump: a pump and dump manipulates price within a market that still functions, while a rug pull removes the market's underlying liquidity or legitimacy entirely.

The clearest version is a liquidity-pool rug pull, where developers control the pool and simply withdraw it, a structural vulnerability of certain token designs rather than a matter of sentiment.

Where people get fooled: audited contracts and locked liquidity get treated as guarantees rather than as reduced risk. Both can be faked or built with loopholes, and the marketing word "audited" has no fixed relationship to how thorough an audit actually was.
Rug pull.usage: A token whose liquidity is suddenly withdrawn by its own developers is described as a rug pull.

Rekt.long:
"Rekt", a deliberate misspelling of wrecked, describes a large, often total, trading loss, particularly one caused by leverage or by liquidation.

The word comes from gaming slang for a decisive defeat and was carried into crypto trading culture, where a leveraged liquidation produces the same abrupt, total-loss experience.

Its casual tone does real work: framing a large loss as a shared joke, rather than as a specific, traceable decision, makes it easier to post about and easier to move past without examining what actually happened.

Where people get fooled: the humour normalises the outcome. Calling a liquidation "getting rekt" files it under bad luck or market cruelty rather than under position sizing or leverage choice, which is usually where the actual cause sits.
Rekt.usage: Traders who lose a leveraged position to liquidation sometimes post about 'getting rekt' rather than detailing the sizing decision that caused it.

Bagholder.long:
A bagholder is someone left holding an asset after its price has collapsed, usually bought near the top and never sold, "holding the bag" as everyone else exited.

The phrase predates any market it is now used in; "left holding the bag" is a much older English idiom for being stuck with the consequences after everyone else has already left.

It is typically used with contempt, aimed at people who held through a decline that looks obvious after the fact, rarely acknowledging that the same decision looked reasonable while it was being made.

Where people get fooled: the mocking tone obscures that becoming a bagholder is usually the endpoint of a slow process, averaging down, refusing to realise a loss, waiting for a recovery, rather than one single bad decision made all at once.
Bagholder.usage: Someone who bought near a peak and held through the entire decline is sometimes called a bagholder, usually by other people.

HODL.long:
HODL means holding an asset through volatility rather than trading it, now commonly backronymed as "hold on for dear life", though that reading arrived after the word already existed.

It originates from a documented typo: a 2013 Bitcointalk forum post titled "I AM HODLING" misspelled holding during a crash, and the community adopted the misspelling as its own term.

As a strategy it describes an intention, not a plan; it says nothing about position size, entry price, or what evidence would change the holder's mind.

Where people get fooled: HODL gets treated as a strategy automatically vindicated by enough time passing, but holding through a decline is only retroactively wise if the asset recovers, and plenty of assets people HODLed never did.
HODL.usage: The term HODL is used to describe holding a position through a drawdown rather than selling, regardless of whether that turns out to be the better outcome.

Diamond / paper hands.long:
"Diamond hands" describes holding a position through severe volatility without selling; "paper hands" describes selling quickly under pressure, often near a low. The pairing frames holding as strength and selling as weakness.

The imagery, diamonds are hard to break, paper tears easily, comes from retail trading forums, notably around the 2021 GameStop episode, where holding through volatility became a point of identity.

The framing treats one behaviour as inherently virtuous, but holding and selling are simply two decisions; which one is correct depends entirely on what happens next, which neither term can know in advance.

Where people get fooled: calling yourself diamond-handed can turn an exit decision into an identity test. Refusing to sell to avoid the "paper hands" label is social pressure, not a risk-management reason, and it can keep a losing position open long after the original thesis has failed.
Diamond / paper hands.usage: Forum posters use 'diamond hands' to praise holding through a drawdown and 'paper hands' to criticise an early exit, independent of whether either decision was actually correct.

Diamond hands / paper hands.long:
"Diamond hands" and "paper hands" carry the same holding-versus-selling pairing as above, phrased with "hands" leading rather than trailing, and used interchangeably with "diamond / paper hands" across different communities.

Both orderings spread from the same retail-trading forum culture, with word order varying by community rather than by meaning; there is no consistent distinction between the two phrasings.

The duplication is itself a small case study in how slang mutates, the same idea reproduced with variant wording as it moves between forums, each community treating its own version as the correct one.

Where people get fooled: because the phrase feels familiar in either order, its repeated use across separate communities can feel like independent confirmation of a shared idea, when it is really the same idea being restated, not re-tested.
Diamond hands / paper hands.usage: The phrase appears as both 'diamond hands / paper hands' and 'diamond / paper hands' across different forums, describing the identical holding-versus-selling framing.

Catching a falling knife.long:
"Catching a falling knife" describes buying an asset while it is still sharply declining, on the expectation that it is near a bottom, the knife metaphor warning that doing so can hurt.

The phrase is an old trading-floor warning, in use across markets long before any specific asset discussed elsewhere in this glossary existed, because the underlying temptation, buying a steep decline, is not new.

It functions as a caution rather than a description of outcome: unlike dip or dead cat bounce, it is usually said before or during a decline, not only after it has finished.

Where people get fooled: a decline that has already fallen a long way feels statistically due to stop, but how far a price has already dropped says nothing about how much further it can still fall. Distance travelled is not distance remaining.
Catching a falling knife.usage: Buying into a sharp, ongoing decline is described as 'catching a falling knife', regardless of whether the purchase later proves well timed.

Stop hunt.long:
A "stop hunt" describes a price move that appears to deliberately trigger clustered stop-loss orders just beyond a visible level, before reversing, implying the move was engineered to trigger them.

Stop orders genuinely do cluster around obvious levels, round numbers, recent highs and lows, and their execution can add a burst of one-directional volume exactly there. That clustering itself is real and observable.

Whether that burst reflects deliberate targeting by another participant, or simply the mechanical result of orders sitting where everyone can see them, is usually impossible to establish from outside the order book.

Where people get fooled: the term assigns intent to what is often just structural mechanics. Visible levels attract visible stops, and a move past them triggers those stops whether or not anyone planned it that way; the label turns a mechanism into an unproven accusation.
Stop hunt.usage: A brief spike beyond an obvious support level that quickly reverses is often called a stop hunt, though intent behind the move is rarely verifiable.

Revenge on the market.long:
"Revenge on the market" is a sarcastic phrase for revenge trading, increasing size or frequency after a loss to try to win the money back quickly, aimed at the market as if it were an opponent.

The market has no memory of the previous loss and no stake in what happens next; the phrase's sarcasm points at the mismatch between the trader's emotional framing and the market's actual indifference.

It is usually said about someone else's behaviour, or one's own in hindsight, rather than declared while it is happening; few people describe themselves as seeking revenge in the moment.

Where people get fooled: the framing of "getting it back" makes a size increase feel like problem-solving rather than what it usually is, a bet made under emotional pressure and with looser criteria than the trade that caused the original loss.
Revenge on the market.usage: Increasing position size immediately after a loss to try to recover it quickly is sometimes described, often self-mockingly, as seeking revenge on the market.

Buy the dip.long:
"Buy the dip" is an instruction derived from the descriptive term dip, treating a pullback within an uptrend as a buying opportunity rather than as a warning.

It became a recognisable slogan during the 2010s bull market in US equities and later crypto, periods when repeated pullbacks were in fact followed by new highs for an extended stretch.

As a rule it has no defined entry criteria, no defined invalidation point, and no defined size; it is a slogan, not a specified, testable strategy that could be measured against alternatives.

Where people get fooled: the phrase's credibility comes entirely from one specific historical stretch when it worked. It carries no assurance the pattern continues, and a rule with no invalidation point cannot tell its user when it has stopped working.
Buy the dip.usage: 'Buy the dip' is used both as a specific instruction to purchase during a pullback and as a general slogan for staying invested through volatility.

To the moon.long:
"To the moon" expresses hope or expectation of a large, dramatic price rise, a prediction phrased as enthusiasm rather than stated as a plain forecast.

The phrase is common across crypto and meme-stock communities, where it doubles as a shared joke and a genuine directional claim, the two often hard to separate from each other.

Dressed as a joke, it still functions as a directional claim; repeating it in a group chat can feel like building a case for a price target no one has actually argued for on the merits.

Where people get fooled: humour lowers the bar for what counts as an argument. Because the phrase is said with a laugh, it escapes the scrutiny a plain price prediction would normally get, even though it makes exactly the same kind of claim.
To the moon.usage: The phrase 'to the moon' is used to express hope or expectation of a large price rise, in both joking and sincere registers.

Alpha decay in public.long:
"Alpha decay in public" describes an edge losing effectiveness because too many people started acting on it after it became widely known, the crowding itself eroding the advantage.

The mechanism follows directly from how markets absorb information: once enough participants trade the same signal, their combined activity moves prices in a way that removes the mispricing the signal depended on.

The "in public" framing distinguishes this from ordinary signal decay, pointing specifically at publication, forum discussion, or social sharing as the trigger, rather than the edge simply expiring on its own timeline.

Where people get fooled: the visible popularity of a strategy gets treated as proof it once worked, when heavy promotion and genuine historical edge are two different things that often travel together for unrelated reasons, one sells content, the other does not need to.
Alpha decay in public.usage: A strategy that stops working shortly after becoming popular on trading forums is sometimes described as having suffered alpha decay in public.

Backtest hero.long:
A "backtest hero" is a strategy, or a person, whose results look exceptional in historical simulation but have never been proven, or have failed, when traded forward with real money.

The gap arises structurally: a backtest can be adjusted and re-run against the same historical data until it looks good, in a way that live trading, happening once and forward only, simply cannot be.

The term is usually aimed at other people's strategies, rarely one's own, which is itself telling about how much more visible the failure mode is from outside than from inside.

Where people get fooled: an impressive backtest is treated as evidence of skill rather than as one output of a search process that, run enough times, will eventually produce something impressive by chance alone regardless of any real edge.
Backtest hero.usage: A strategy praised for its backtest performance but untested or unsuccessful in live trading is sometimes dismissed as a 'backtest hero'.

Blown up.long:
To be "blown up" means to have lost a large share, or all, of a trading account, typically abruptly, often through leverage or a position that was not appropriately sized.

The term borrows the imagery of an explosion, sudden and total, which fits how leveraged losses actually behave: they can move from manageable to account-ending within a single sharp move.

It is used both as plain description, "the account blew up", and informally as a badge, some traders frame surviving a blow-up as a rite of passage rather than as a preventable error.

Where people get fooled: framing a blow-up as an inevitable part of paying tuition can obscure that most blow-ups trace back to one identifiable decision, oversized leverage, no stop, no position limit, rather than to bad luck alone.
Blown up.usage: An account that loses most or all of its capital in a short period, often via leverage, is described as having 'blown up'.

Chop.long:
"Chop" describes sideways, directionless price action with no sustained trend, moves up, then down, over a similar range, without net progress in either direction.

The word reflects how the price action feels to trade: frequent small reversals that chop up a position, often triggering stops or exits on both sides of the same range in succession.

It is a shape description applied in real time as well as in hindsight, unlike most other slang here, because sideways range-bound movement is often visible while it is happening, not only afterwards.

Where people get fooled: trend-following methods perform worst during chop, and chop is common, so a string of losses during choppy conditions gets misread as a broken strategy rather than as the expected, if uncomfortable, cost of being trend-following at all.
Chop.usage: A market moving sideways within a range for an extended period is described as 'chop', a condition that erodes trend-following systems in particular.

Fade.long:
To "fade" a move is to trade against it, selling into a rally or buying into a decline, on the expectation of a reversal rather than a continuation of the existing move.

The term comes from a price move losing momentum, fading, with a trader positioning for that loss of momentum before it happens, essentially betting on mean reversion within a specific move.

"Fade the news", "fade the crowd": the phrase extends beyond price action to fading whatever the majority appears to be doing, treating popularity itself as a contrarian signal worth acting on.

Where people get fooled: fading strong momentum works often enough, in choppy conditions, to build false confidence, then fails badly and rarely, during genuine trends, the same behaviour producing a long run of small wins followed by one large loss.
Fade.usage: A trader who sells into a sharp rally, expecting it to lose momentum, is said to be fading the move.

Printing.long:
"Printing" describes making consistent, often large, profits, "the strategy is printing", borrowing the image of a printing press producing money on demand.

The phrase gained wider circulation from "money printer go brr" internet culture around central bank quantitative easing, then generalised to any source of reliably repeating gains.

It is almost always used in the present tense, mid-streak, which is exactly the period in which a run of good results is least distinguishable from a run of ordinary good luck.

Where people get fooled: a live winning streak gets described as printing well before there is enough trade history to separate skill from variance, and the phrase itself, implying automatic and repeatable output, discourages that check from happening at all.
Printing.usage: A strategy or trader on a run of consistent gains is often described as 'printing', usually before the sample size is large enough to say anything about repeatability.

Melt-up.long:
A "melt-up" is a sustained, unusually fast price rise not obviously explained by news or fundamentals, often driven by participants buying simply because the price is rising and they fear missing out.

The mechanism is self-reinforcing: rising prices attract new buyers, whose buying pushes prices further, drawing in still more buyers, a feedback loop similar to a short squeeze but driven by fresh buying rather than forced covering.

Unlike a blow-off top, melt-up does not necessarily imply an imminent reversal; it can describe an ongoing, ambiguous state rather than only the peak moment of one.

Where people get fooled: a melt-up feels, from inside, indistinguishable from the early stage of a durable structural change in an asset's value. Only the outcome, whether the rise holds or fully retraces, settles which one it was, and that is known only afterwards.
Melt-up.usage: A rapid, broad-based price rise without a clear fundamental driver is described as a melt-up while it is still in progress.

Exit liquidity.long:
"Exit liquidity" describes buyers whose purchases allow earlier holders to sell, the buyers providing the liquidity that lets someone else exit, often without realising that is the role they are playing.

The term encodes a real structural observation: every sale needs a buyer on the other side, and in a declining or topping asset, later buyers are mechanically the ones enabling earlier holders' exits.

It is most often used as an accusation, "retail is exit liquidity for the smart money", which adds a claim about who is informed and who is not on top of the plain structural fact.

Where people get fooled: the structural part is true of every trade, in every market, at all times, there is always someone on the other side. The added claim, that one group is systematically informed and another systematically not, needs separate evidence the phrase does not itself supply.
Exit liquidity.usage: The phrase 'exit liquidity' describes buyers who unknowingly enable earlier holders to sell, though the added claim about who is better informed is usually asserted rather than demonstrated.

Degen.long:
"Degen", short for degenerate, is used, often self-mockingly, for high-risk, low-diligence trading or gambling-like behaviour, particularly in crypto: unresearched tokens, high leverage, or both together.

The term is worn as a badge within some communities rather than treated as a warning, turning what is structurally closer to gambling into an in-group identity worth signalling.

Self-labelling as degen is sometimes used pre-emptively, a way of disclaiming responsibility for a bet before making it, the label absorbing the criticism in advance.

Where people get fooled: calling a trade degen as a joke can make genuinely poor risk management feel like a knowing, ironic choice rather than an actual mistake, which removes some of the discomfort that would otherwise prompt a change in behaviour.
Degen.usage: Traders sometimes label their own high-risk, low-diligence bets 'degen' as a way of acknowledging the risk while still making the trade.

Send it.long:
"Send it" is an exclamation used to encourage entering a trade, usually a risky or oversized one, without further deliberation, action prioritised over analysis.

The phrase comes from extreme-sports culture, sending it off a jump or drop, and was adopted into trading and crypto slang for the same all-in, commit-now attitude.

It functions socially as encouragement within a group, which is part of what makes it effective at overriding an individual's own hesitation; the pressure comes from other people, not from any new information about the trade.

Where people get fooled: hesitation before a trade is sometimes a genuine, informative signal that something about the position is not fully thought through. "Send it" treats that hesitation as an obstacle to overcome rather than as information worth checking first.
Send it.usage: 'Send it' is used, often in a group chat, to encourage taking a trade immediately rather than deliberating further.

Sim / paper.long:
"Sim" or "paper" trading means executing trades in a simulated environment with no real money at risk, used to test a strategy's logic or to practise execution mechanics.

The mechanism strips out capital risk but keeps price movement and, in good implementations, order mechanics, which is useful for testing logic but removes the psychological pressure that real capital creates.

Results from sim trading are frequently presented, informally, as evidence of skill or a validated strategy, without noting that the environment differs from live trading in exactly the dimension, genuine loss aversion, that most affects decisions.

Where people get fooled: performance in sim does not reliably predict performance live, because the hardest part of trading for most people is behavioural, under real financial pressure, and that pressure is precisely what sim trading leaves out.
Sim / paper.usage: A track record built entirely in sim or paper trading is often shared as if it demonstrates live-trading skill, despite the absence of real capital at risk.

Outcome bias.long:
Outcome bias is judging the quality of a decision by how it turned out rather than by the information and reasoning actually available at the time the decision was made.

A good decision can still lose, and a poor one can still win. Outcome bias collapses that distinction, treating every profitable trade as evidence of a good process and every loss as evidence of a bad one.

It runs in both directions: a reckless trade that happens to work gets remembered as skill, while a well-reasoned trade that loses gets remembered as a mistake, regardless of what the odds actually were beforehand.

Where people get fooled: a trading journal that records only outcomes, not the reasoning and conditions present at entry, cannot separate process from luck later. The fix is structural, writing the thesis and criteria down before the outcome is known, not simply trying harder to think objectively afterwards.
Outcome bias.usage: Reviewing a trade by asking only 'did it work' rather than 'was the reasoning sound at the time' is a description of outcome bias in practice.

Overconfidence after a win streak.long:
A run of winning trades can inflate a trader's sense of their own skill beyond what the sample size actually supports, leading to larger positions or looser risk control on the trades that follow.

The mechanism is a small-sample problem: short winning streaks are common even from a strategy with no real edge, purely from variance, but they feel, from inside, like earned confirmation.

The behavioural shift is often visible in position sizing before it shows up anywhere else, size increases quietly, justified as "the strategy is working", well before enough data exists to support that conclusion.

Where people get fooled: confidence rises with each win, but the statistical case for genuine edge needs far more trades than a typical streak provides. Sizing that stays fixed regardless of recent results is the direct countermeasure; awareness of the bias alone does not stop it operating.
Overconfidence after a win streak.usage: Increasing position size specifically because of a recent winning streak, rather than because of any new information, describes overconfidence after a win streak.

Analysis paralysis.long:
Analysis paralysis is the state of gathering and re-checking information to the point that no decision gets made, or a decision is made too late to act on.

It often stems from treating more analysis as always safer, when in trading a delayed entry or exit is itself a decision with its own consequences, not a neutral, risk-free default option.

The pattern frequently coexists with a fear of being wrong that no additional chart or indicator can fully resolve, so the search for certainty continues past the point where it would actually change the decision.

Where people get fooled: each additional check feels like it is reducing risk, but past a certain point it is only delaying a decision that has to be made regardless. A predefined checklist and entry criteria, set before looking at the current chart, is the structural countermeasure.
Analysis paralysis.usage: Repeatedly re-checking the same setup without executing, until the entry opportunity has passed, describes analysis paralysis.

Screen time.long:
Screen time refers to the amount of time a trader spends watching live price action, distinct from time spent on research, review, or system development away from a live chart.

Extended screen time increases exposure to short-term noise, and more exposure to noise creates more opportunities to react to moves that a slower, systematic process would simply have ignored.

It is not identical to overtrading, but the two are connected: watching a chart continuously creates pressure to act on it continuously, even when the underlying strategy does not call for frequent decisions.

Where people get fooled: more hours watching the market feels like more diligence, but for most strategies with a defined holding period, extra screen time mainly adds intervention opportunities rather than useful information. Bounding when the chart gets checked, in advance, does more than trying to simply watch less.
Screen time.usage: The amount of time spent watching a live chart, as distinct from research or review time, is what 'screen time' refers to.

Availability heuristic.long:
The availability heuristic is judging how likely or common something is by how easily examples come to mind, rather than by its actual documented frequency.

The bias was documented by Tversky and Kahneman: vivid, recent, or emotionally charged events are recalled more easily and are therefore judged more probable, independent of their real base rate.

In trading, a recent large win or loss, one's own or a widely shared story, becomes disproportionately influential on the next decision, simply because it is the example most readily recalled.

Where people get fooled: a single vivid outcome, positive or negative, gets weighted like a trend rather than as one data point. Working from a written record of actual trade outcomes, rather than from memory, is the structural countermeasure, since memory is selectively vivid in a way a log is not.
Availability heuristic.usage: Judging a setup as reliable mainly because a recent, memorable example of it worked is an instance of the availability heuristic.

Base rate neglect.long:
Base rate neglect is ignoring the general, underlying frequency of an outcome in favour of specific-seeming details about the current situation.

In trading this shows up as treating a setup's apparent quality, how clean the chart looks, how confident the reasoning feels, as more informative than its actual historical hit rate and payoff.

It compounds with the narrative fallacy: a compelling story about why this time is different feels like it should override the base rate, when the base rate is exactly what a compelling story tends to obscure.

Where people get fooled: a setup that "looks textbook" gets traded with more confidence than its measured history justifies, because the visual pattern is vivid and the base rate is abstract. Checking the measured frequency before acting, as a fixed step, counters the pull of how convincing the current case feels.
Base rate neglect.usage: Trading a setup with more confidence because it 'looks textbook' than its actual measured historical performance would justify describes base rate neglect.

Narrative fallacy.long:
The narrative fallacy is the tendency to prefer a coherent story that explains events over a more accurate, but messier, account of what actually happened or why.

Financial commentary supplies a fresh narrative for almost every price move after the fact, which creates a false sense that markets are more explicable, and more predictable, than they typically are.

In trading, a setup wrapped in a compelling story, a plausible-sounding reason it should work, gets trusted more readily than one presented as a plain, unexplained statistical pattern, even when the statistical case is identical.

Where people get fooled: a good story about why a trade should work substitutes for actual evidence that it does. Testing whether a rationale's implied statistical claim actually holds up out of sample is the check the story itself cannot provide, however plausible it sounds.
Narrative fallacy.usage: Being persuaded by a compelling explanation of a past price move, more than by the underlying data, is the narrative fallacy in operation.

Herding.long:
Herding is following the crowd's behaviour or positioning rather than independent analysis, buying because others are buying, selling because others are selling.

It can be a rational response to genuine information other participants might hold, but in trading it is frequently driven by social proof and fear of missing out rather than any real information advantage.

Herding tends to intensify at extremes; the most crowded trades often cluster near tops and bottoms, precisely because that is when social pressure to join is strongest.

Where people get fooled: a crowded trade feels safer because so many others hold the same view, but shared conviction is not the same as a shared information edge, and a crowd that has to unwind together can move price sharply on the way out.
Herding.usage: Increasing exposure to a position mainly because it has become widely popular, rather than because of new independent analysis, describes herding.

Illusion of control.long:
The illusion of control is overestimating one's ability to influence outcomes that are actually driven by chance or by forces outside one's control.

In trading it shows up as attributing a winning streak to skill in reading the market, or believing that watching a position more closely, or intervening more actively, changes the odds of the outcome.

Discretionary adjustments made mid-trade, moving a stop, adding size, exiting early, are sometimes driven less by new information than by a felt need to be doing something in response to uncertainty.

Where people get fooled: the feeling of active control is comforting under uncertainty, but comfort is not evidence the intervention improved anything. A pre-committed rule set, followed regardless of how the trade feels while open, removes the chance for felt control to override the plan.
Illusion of control.usage: Believing that closely monitoring an open position improves its outcome, independent of any new information, describes the illusion of control.

Dunning-Kruger in trading.long:
The Dunning-Kruger effect describes low-skill individuals overestimating their competence, because the same lack of skill that limits performance also limits the ability to judge that performance accurately.

The effect is genuinely documented in Kruger and Dunning's original research, though it is also widely overstated in popular use, applied more broadly and more confidently than the original findings actually support.

In trading, early success, often from a favourable market regime rather than skill, can produce a strong sense of competence before enough varied experience exists to reveal what is not yet understood.

Where people get fooled: the mismatch is invisible from inside the early stage, feeling confident is not evidence of being competent, and it is also not reliable evidence of the opposite. A track record measured across different market regimes, not just one favourable one, is the closest available check.
Dunning-Kruger in trading.usage: Early trading confidence built during a single favourable market regime, before it has been tested across others, is sometimes discussed in relation to Dunning-Kruger, cautiously given how often the effect is overstated.

Fear of missing out.long:
Fear of missing out, or FOMO, is entering a trade primarily because of a fear of being left out of a move already in progress, rather than because of independent analysis.

The mechanism runs on loss aversion applied to a gain that has not happened yet, the discomfort of watching others profit is processed in a similar way to the discomfort of an actual loss.

FOMO entries characteristically arrive late in a move, after most of the visible gain has already occurred, and with less regard for defined risk than a planned entry would carry.

Where people get fooled: the urgency feels like it is coming from the market, a closing window, but it is generated internally, by the discomfort of comparison with others. A rule that a missed setup is simply missed, with no late chase permitted, is the structural countermeasure.
Fear of missing out.usage: Entering a position specifically because a move is already underway and others appear to be profiting from it describes FOMO.

Regret aversion.long:
Regret aversion is making decisions specifically to avoid the anticipated feeling of regret, rather than to optimise the actual expected outcome of the decision itself.

In trading it shows up as holding a losing position to avoid the regret of selling near a low, or avoiding a trade entirely to avoid the regret of a loss, even when the expected value favours acting.

It also affects exits from winners: taking profit too early to lock in a gain and avoid the regret of watching it disappear, even when the original thesis for holding longer is still intact.

Where people get fooled: the anticipated regret of a wrong decision gets weighted more heavily than the anticipated regret of a missed opportunity, though both are just imagined future feelings, not information about the trade. Rules fixed before entry remove the in-the-moment weighing of one against the other.
Regret aversion.usage: Holding a losing position specifically to avoid the discomfort of selling near a low, rather than because the original thesis still holds, describes regret aversion.

Mental accounting.long:
Mental accounting is treating money differently depending on its source or the category assigned to it, rather than as fungible, the same unit valued differently in different mental buckets.

The concept was developed by Richard Thaler; in trading, a common version is treating profits as "house money" to be risked more freely than the capital originally deposited.

It also appears as separating a strategy's gains from its losses into different mental accounts, rather than tracking the combined, net result, celebrating winning trades in isolation from the losses that sit alongside them.

Where people get fooled: house money feels less real to lose than the original deposit, which leads to looser risk-taking with profits than the account's total exposure would justify. Sizing decisions off the account's total value, not its labelled sub-parts, is the structural fix.
Mental accounting.usage: Taking larger risks with recent profits than would be taken with the original deposit, on the reasoning that it is 'house money', describes mental accounting.

Boredom trading.long:
Boredom trading is taking a trade primarily to relieve boredom or the discomfort of inactivity, rather than because a valid setup under a defined strategy has actually occurred.

It is most likely during quiet, low-opportunity market conditions, when a trader accustomed to frequent action starts lowering their own criteria simply to have something to do.

The trades produced this way typically fall outside a strategy's actual rules, even when the trader can construct a plausible-sounding reason for the entry after the fact.

Where people get fooled: the discomfort of inactivity gets mistaken for a signal that something needs to be done, when it is actually just discomfort. A rule that no valid setup means no trade, with sizing on any "just to do something" trade set at zero, is the structural fix.
Boredom trading.usage: Taking a trade during a quiet market mainly to relieve inactivity, without a setup meeting the usual criteria, describes boredom trading.

Identity and trading.long:
This describes trading becoming part of a person's self-image, "I am a trader" rather than "I do some trading", which changes what a losing trade, or a losing period, threatens.

When trading is identity, a loss is no longer just a financial outcome; it becomes information, or feels like information, about the person's competence or worth, raising the stakes of every decision.

This tends to make it harder to exit a failing strategy or admit a period of underperformance, because doing so can feel like an admission about the self rather than a routine, expected part of trading.

Where people get fooled: decisions that should be made on the numbers get filtered instead through what a given choice implies about who the person is. Keeping results and self-worth explicitly separate, and maintaining other sources of identity outside the market, is the structural countermeasure.
Identity and trading.usage: Feeling that a losing streak reflects personally on one's competence, rather than being a routine and expected part of any strategy's results, is what 'identity and trading' points to.

Isolation.long:
Isolation describes the tendency of trading, especially discretionary or solo systematic trading, to be done alone, without the outside checks that come from colleagues or a team reviewing decisions.

A trading desk in an institutional setting has natural checks, a manager, a risk desk, colleagues who ask questions. A solo trader working from home has none of that built in by default.

Isolation compounds other biases on this list, because there is no one else present to question a rationalisation, point out a pattern of repeated mistakes, or notice tilt developing in real time.

Where people get fooled: working alone feels neutral, simply a mode of working, but it removes a check that most professional trading environments build in deliberately. A trading journal reviewed by someone else, or a small peer group, substitutes for the check isolation otherwise removes.
Isolation.usage: Trading alone, without a colleague, mentor, or peer group reviewing decisions, is what 'isolation' refers to in this context.

Expectation setting.long:
Expectation setting is establishing, in advance, a realistic range of outcomes for a strategy or trading period, based on its actual measured history rather than on hope or a best-case scenario.

Without it, ordinary variance, a losing week within a strategy that has a genuine long-run edge, gets interpreted as failure, because the trader's internal benchmark for "normal" was never actually defined.

Properly set expectations use the strategy's own drawdown history and win-versus-loss distribution, not a single best-case backtest run, since one run understates how much variation is genuinely normal.

Where people get fooled: a drawdown well within a strategy's historical range still feels alarming without a pre-set expectation for what that range looks like. Writing down the expected drawdown and losing-streak length before trading begins gives a fixed reference the in-the-moment feeling can be checked against.
Expectation setting.usage: Writing down a strategy's expected drawdown range in advance, based on its measured history, is an example of expectation setting.

Detachment from money.long:
Detachment from money describes treating the numbers in a trading account as units to be managed correctly, rather than as their real-world equivalent in rent, bills, or savings, a deliberate distancing, not indifference.

The aim is to reduce the emotional charge attached to each fluctuation, since strong emotional reactions to normal account variance tend to produce worse decisions, not better ones.

It is easy to overstate as advice, "just don't care about the money", which misses that the actual mechanism is sizing risk small enough, relative to total capital and to life circumstances, that any single outcome carries little weight.

Where people get fooled: detachment gets treated as a mental trick to be willed into existence, when it is mostly a downstream effect of position sizing. Risking an amount that would not meaningfully affect daily life if lost is the structural route to it; trying to simply feel less rarely works alone.
Detachment from money.usage: Sizing a position so that its outcome would not meaningfully affect daily finances either way is the structural route toward detachment from money, rather than a mindset adopted directly.

The first big win problem.long:
The first big win problem describes how an early, unusually large or lucky win can distort a trader's baseline expectations for what normal performance looks like, well before enough experience exists to calibrate.

A large early win, often the product of favourable timing or an unrepeatable market condition rather than a repeatable process, becomes the internal benchmark against which every later result gets measured, and most later results compare unfavourably.

It also tends to raise the position sizes a trader is comfortable with going forward, anchored to what worked once, rather than to what a properly sized, repeatable strategy actually supports.

Where people get fooled: the emotional force of a first large win is disproportionate to its statistical significance, one outcome, however large, is a sample size of one. Reviewing it explicitly as an outlier, before it sets expectations, is the structural check.
The first big win problem.usage: An unusually large early trading win becoming the benchmark for what normal performance should look like afterwards describes the first big win problem.
